title: Trees that predict numbers
objectives: Fit a regression tree and read its step-shaped predictions.
Say when a tree beats a line and why it cannot extrapolate.

screens.title: One number for a group
screens.prose: Eight trading days: yesterday's realised volatility across, today's down. A tree has already split them at 20.5%. Each side must forecast one number for its days. The right side's level, 24%, is set; drag the left level.

derive.caption: Left level {{fixed(L.y, 1)}}%: squared error on the left days {{fixed(pow(11 - L.y, 2)+pow(13 - L.y, 2)+pow(12 - L.y, 2)+pow(16 - L.y, 2), 1)}}

screens.question: Drag the left level to make the squared error on the left days as small as possible.

hints.text: Watch the caption as you drag: it adds the four squared gaps.
Too high or too low, one side's gaps grow fast. Look for the balance point.
The four left days are 11, 13, 12 and 16. Their mean is 13.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep dragging until the caption's squared error stops falling.

byKey.median: 12.5 is the median of the four days. Squared error is smallest at the mean, 13.
byKey.high: The level sits above most of the left days. Pull it down until the gaps balance.

explain.text: The squared error bottoms out at 13%, the mean of 11, 13, 12 and 16. A regression tree's leaf forecasts the mean of its training rows. The right side's 24% is the mean of its four days too.

screens.title: Where to split
screens.prose: Before splitting, one level for all eight days, their mean of 18.5%, leaves a squared error of 270. Each candidate split gives each side its own mean. The table lists the squared error left.

state.caption: Total of both sides' squared errors around their own means.

screens.question: Tap the split a regression tree would choose.

hints.text: The tree wants the split that removes the most squared error.
Look for the smallest number in the right column.
At 20.5% only 28 is left: a drop of 242 from 270.

feedback.correct: 20.5%: it cuts the squared error from 270 to 28.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the row with the least squared error left.

byKey.r4: 24% puts the day at 22% with the high days. 124.8 is left, far more than at 20.5%.
byKey.r6: 32% splits off one day. The big jump between 19% and 22% stays inside one side.

explain.text: Splitting at 20.5% leaves 28 of the 270, a drop of 242. For regression, this drop in squared error plays the part Gini's gain played for classes. scikit-learn's `DecisionTreeRegressor` picks the same 20.5%.

screens.title: Steps
screens.prose: A tree on 200 days from `make_vol(1, 300)`, using yesterday's vol only; 120 of the days are plotted. Each leaf is an interval of yesterday's vol with one forecast. Slide the depth.
screens.question: At depth 3, how many different forecasts can the tree give?

hints.text: Count the flat steps at depth 3.
Each leaf gives one step.
Three levels of yes-or-no questions give $2^3 = 8$ leaves.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the horizontal steps at depth 3.

byKey.three: 3 is the depth. Each level doubles the leaves: $2^3$.
byKey.six: Count again at depth 3; some steps are short.

explain.text: A regression tree's forecast is a **step function**: flat within each leaf, jumping at each threshold. Depth 2 already finds the three regimes near 16% and 26%; deeper trees add small steps that chase noise. Test MSE is 7.04 at depth 2, 7.02 at depth 3 and 7.80 at depth 4.

screens.title: Leaf size smooths
screens.prose: Now remove the depth limit and set a floor on leaf size instead. Setting 1 is `min_samples_leaf=1`, setting 2 is 10 and setting 3 is 40.
screens.question: With `min_samples_leaf=1` and no depth limit, what does the tree forecast for a day it was trained on?

options.text: That day's own value, since its leaf holds that day alone

options.why: That is a tree with no splits at all. With no limit, each leaf shrinks to a single day.

options.text: The mean of its regime, about 12%, 20% or 32%
options.why: That is what depth 2 gives. With no limit the tree keeps splitting past the regimes.

options.text: Nothing: a leaf needs at least two rows
options.why: A leaf may hold one row; it forecasts that row's value.

hints.text: How small can a leaf get with a floor of 1?
A leaf with one day has that day as its mean.
With no limit each training day ends alone in a leaf, so the forecast equals its own value.

feedback.correct: One day per leaf: the forecast copies it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is the mean of a leaf holding one day?

explain.text: A floor of 1 gives 197 leaves and a near-zero training MSE of 0.16, but a test MSE of 13.9. A floor of 40 leaves 4 leaves and a test MSE of 7.04. Leaf size works as a smoothing control.

screens.title: Beyond the data
screens.prose: The training days had yesterday's vol between 8% and 40%. In a crisis it reaches 60%. The depth-3 tree and a fitted line, $3.051 + 0.8356x$, both forecast today's vol.
screens.question: What does the tree forecast at 60%?

options.why: You expected the tree to extend the trend. That is the line. A tree's last leaf covers everything above its last threshold.

options.text: No forecast: 60% is outside the data
options.why: The tree always answers. Every value above its last threshold falls in the last leaf.
That one day is averaged with the others in its leaf. The leaf mean is the forecast.

hints.text: Which leaf does a day at 60% fall into?
Every question compares vol with a threshold below 40%. A day at 60% answers each one the same as a day at 40%.
It lands in the rightmost leaf, which forecasts that leaf's mean.

feedback.correct: 35.71%: the forecast is flat beyond the data.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow a day at 60% through the tree's thresholds.

byKey.trend: You expected the tree to extrapolate. It cannot: past 40% it repeats its last leaf's mean.

explain.text: A tree cannot extrapolate. Above its last threshold the forecast stays at 35.71%, and it can never exceed the largest training target. The line forecasts 53.19%, which may be too high, but it at least moves.

screens.title: Steps or a line?
screens.prose: Two seeded data sets of 100 rows, 60 to train and 40 to test. In `make_linear` the target rises steadily with $x$. In `make_step` it jumps by 12 at $x = 25$. Both models fit each set.
screens.question: Which reading of the table is right?

options.text: The line wins on the steady data; the tree wins on the jump
The tree wins on both, because it is the more flexible model
options.why: On the steady data its steps miss the slope: 17.24 against 10.29. Flexibility only helps where the shape needs it.

options.text: The line wins on both, because trees overfit
options.why: On the jump the line has to smear a step into a slope: 21.42 against 11.46.
The gaps are large, about 7 and 10 units of MSE, on 40 test rows each.

hints.text: Compare the models row by row.
Row 1: 17.24 against 10.29. Row 2: 11.46 against 21.42.
Each model wins where its shape matches the truth.

feedback.correct: Match the model's shape to the data's shape.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two numbers in each row separately.

explain.text: With 60 rows, the tree's eight steps approximate a straight line badly, so the line wins on smooth data. On a threshold effect, the tree puts its first split near 25 and the line cannot bend. Trees win on jumps and regimes, lines on steady slopes.

screens.title: Why the mean
screens.prose: On screen 1 you found that the mean minimises squared error. Prove it for a leaf with values $y_1, \dots, y_n$ and a forecast $c$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $S(c) = \sum_i (y_i - c)^2$, the squared error of forecast $c$
$S'(c) = 0 \Rightarrow \sum_i y_i = n c$, setting the slope to zero

hints.text: Start from what we minimise.
Differentiate, then set the derivative to zero.
Definition, derivative, set to zero, solve for $c$, check the second derivative.

feedback.correct: The leaf mean is the best constant under squared error.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Define, differentiate, solve, then check it is a minimum.

byKey.min: The second-derivative check comes after finding $c$.

explain.text: $S(c)$ is a parabola in $c$ with its lowest point at $\bar y$. So every leaf forecasts its mean. A split's value is how far it lowers the total of the leaves' $S(\bar y)$.

screens.title: A one-split tree by hand
screens.prose: Code the tree from screens 1 and 2. Rows with $x$ at most the threshold form the left leaf, the rest the right. Each leaf forecasts its mean.
screens.question: Complete `leaf_mean_predict`, rounding each forecast to 6 places.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_vol(seed, n=300):
    """n days: yesterday's realised vol (%, annualised) and volume (z-score);
    target: next day's realised vol (%). Three calm-to-stressed regimes."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    vol = np.round(rng.uniform(8, 40, n), 2)
    volume = np.round(rng.standard_normal(n), 2)
    level = np.where(vol < 16, 12.0, np.where(vol < 26, 20.0, 32.0))
    y = np.round(level + 1.5 * (volume > 1) + rng.normal(0, 2.5, n), 2)
    return np.column_stack([vol, volume]), y

def make_linear(seed, n=100):
    """One feature x in [8, 40]; target 4 + 0.8 x plus noise."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = np.round(rng.uniform(8, 40, n), 2)
    y = np.round(4 + 0.8 * x + rng.normal(0, 3, n), 2)
    return x.reshape(-1, 1), y

def make_step(seed, n=100):
    """One feature x in [8, 40]; target jumps by 12 at x = 25."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = np.round(rng.uniform(8, 40, n), 2)
    y = np.round(14 + 12 * (x > 25) + rng.normal(0, 3, n), 2)
    return x.reshape(-1, 1), y

def leaf_mean_predict(x_train, y_train, threshold,
                      x_query):
    pairs = list(zip(x_train, y_train))
    left = [y for x, y in pairs if x <= threshold]
    right = [y for x, y in pairs if x > threshold]
    mean_left = sum(left) / len(left)
    mean_right = sum(right) / len(right)
    return [round(mean_left if q <= threshold else mean_right, 6)
            for q in x_query]

screens.title: The drop in squared error
screens.prose: Score a split as the tree does. Take the parent's squared error around its mean, minus each side's squared error around its own mean.
screens.question: Complete `sse_gain`, rounded to 6 places.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, each worked by hand. They cover the eight days, small splits, a constant target and a split that moves no rows. Values are compared with math.isclose.

hints.text: Use the `sse` helper three times.
Parent first, then subtract each side.
`round(sse(parent) - sse(list(y_left)) - sse(list(y_right)), 6)`.

feedback.correct: 242 for the eight days, as the table showed.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Subtract both sides' squared errors from the parent's, each around its own mean.

explain.text: A constant target gains 0 from every split, so the tree stays a single leaf. Dividing the gain by $n$ gives the drop in MSE, which is how scikit-learn's `criterion="squared_error"` reports it. The best split is the same either way.

from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

def tree_vs_line_mse(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test,
                     depth):
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
    line = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train)
    tree_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, tree.predict(X_test))
    line_mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, line.predict(X_test))
    return round(float(tree_mse), 4), round(float(line_mse), 4)

screens.title: A volatility forecast in a crisis
screens.prose: A risk desk forecasts tomorrow's realised vol with a depth-2 tree on yesterday's vol and volume, fitted on 200 days. On those days realised vol ran from about 3% to 39%. Today yesterday's vol was 80% and volume 4 standard deviations high.
screens.question: What does the tree forecast for tomorrow?

hints.text: Follow the questions from the top.
Vol 80 is above 26.0, then above 33.0.
That leaf forecasts 31.2.

feedback.correct: 31.2%: lower than the 32.7% leaf, and far below 80%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Answer each question for vol 80 and read the leaf's value.

byKey.max: 32.7 is the leaf for vol between 26 and 33. A day at 80 answers yes to vol > 33.0.
byKey.eighty: A tree never forecasts beyond its leaves' means. Its largest leaf here is 32.7.

explain.text: The forecast is 31.2%, the mean of the stressed leaf. A tree's forecast never exceeds its largest leaf mean, here 32.7%, itself below the largest training day, 38.8%. In a crisis beyond the data it understates risk: pair it with a model that extrapolates, or a hard floor.

ideas: A regression tree forecasts the mean of its leaf; it splits where the drop in squared error is largest.
Its forecast is a step function: depth and leaf size set how many steps, and too many steps chase noise.
It cannot extrapolate: beyond the data the forecast is flat, and it never exceeds the largest training target.

formula.name: Squared-error gain
formula.tex: \Delta = \sum_{i \in P} (y_i - \bar y_P)^2 - \sum_{i \in L} (y_i - \bar y_L)^2 - \sum_{i \in R} (y_i - \bar y_R)^2
formula.note: Each leaf forecasts its own mean.

summary.trap: Expecting a tree to continue a trend beyond the training range; its forecast stays at the last leaf's mean.

quiz.prose: Every training row has the same target, 15%.
quiz.question: What tree does `DecisionTreeRegressor()` grow?

options.text: A full tree, one leaf per row
options.why: No split lowers the squared error, which is already 0, so the root never splits.

options.text: An error: there is nothing to learn
options.why: No error is raised; the tree is a single leaf.

feedback.correct: One leaf: no split can gain anything.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What is the squared error at the root?

explain.text: The root's squared error is already 0, so every split gains 0 and the tree stops. It forecasts 15% everywhere.

quiz.prose: A leaf holds four days with next-day vol 18%, 22%, 19% and 25%.
quiz.question: What does the leaf forecast?

widget.label: Leaf forecast
widget.accept: 21: the mean of the four days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A regression leaf forecasts the mean of its training targets.

byKey.median: 20.5 is the median. Squared error is minimised by the mean.
byKey.mid: 21.5 is halfway between the smallest and largest. Use all four values.

explain.text: $(18 + 22 + 19 + 25)/4 = 21$. The mean minimises the squared error inside the leaf.

quiz.prose: You have 40 days and a target that rises steadily with one feature. A colleague fits a depth-4 tree.
quiz.question: What do you expect against a straight line?

options.text: The line forecasts better: 16 steps over 40 rows chase noise and miss the slope
The tree, since more leaves track the slope more closely
options.why: With 40 rows each of 16 leaves holds 2 or 3 days, so its steps are mostly noise.

options.text: The same: both fit the training data well
options.why: Training fit is not the test. The tree fits its 40 rows better and new days worse.

feedback.correct: Steps everywhere lose to a line on a smooth slope.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many rows would each of the 16 leaves hold?

explain.text: On `make_linear(1)` even a depth-3 tree on 60 rows lost to the line, 17.24 against 10.29. With fewer rows and more leaves it gets worse.

quiz.prose: A regression tree was trained on days whose next-day vol ranged from 9% to 41%.
quiz.question: Which forecast is impossible for it?

options.why: 9% is possible only if a leaf held that one day alone; it is not impossible.
25% could be a leaf mean of days on either side of it.
A leaf holding only days near the top could average 40%.

feedback.correct: No leaf mean can exceed the largest training value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A forecast is a mean of training targets.

explain.text: Each forecast is the mean of some training targets, so it lies between 9% and 41%. A tree cannot forecast a crisis worse than any it has seen.
